Top of the Morning
By Ryan Barwick
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios
 

Swings in food prices have opened M&A windows across America's grocery aisles, writes Axios Pro's Ryan Barwick.

The big picture: Grocery inflation is relatively muted compared with the broader CPI, but price trends are diverging sharply across categories.

Zoom in: Price cycles can quickly juice — or crush — a food company's earnings, giving owners an incentive to sell into strength and buyers an opportunity to bet on a rebound.

Case in point: Kingswood hired North Point to sell Branding Iron less than two years after buying it, Axios has learned, as a cattle shortage has boosted beef prices and earnings.

  • On the other side, pastured-egg company Vital Farms is exploring strategic alternatives after the egg market swung from shortage to oversupply.
  • Chicken too, is becoming a hot commodity amongst private equity investors.

By the numbers: PE deals for packaged-food and meat producers totaled $5.92 billion through July — nearly matching the $6.75 billion recorded during all of 2025, per S&P.

  • Median deal size jumped nearly 80%, even as the number of transactions declined to 140 from 264 in the same period.
  • The biggest deals so far this year include CVC's purchase of flavor and fragrance giant IFF for $4.3 billion and Warburg Pincus' $1 billion investment in Global Eggs.

Zoom out: Beyond beef and eggs, buyers are also circling premium staples brands with proven pricing power.

  • Strategics have been snapping up brands like mac-and-cheese maker Goodles and granola maker Purely Elizabeth, while squeeze-bottle olive oil brand Graza hired Lazard to explore a sale.

The bottom line: The question for buyers is how much of today's EBITDA will sustain until tomorrow.
 
 
The BFD
By Lucinda Shen
 

Illustration: Shoshana Gordon/Axios
 

Israel's Finance Ministry is objecting to the $4.2 billion sale of ZIM, its largest shipping company to Germany's Hapag-Lloyd, in part due to Saudi Arabian and Qatari holdings in the latter.

Why it's the BFD: Ocean routes are uniquely important to Israel, with the "vast majority" of its international trade via water.

Context: This also comes despite a recent secret meeting between top military commanders from the U.S., Israel, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar to discuss tensions in the region.

Driving the news: The ministry pointed to the "involvement of hostile shareholders" as one of the reasons for objecting to the deal, noting Qatar and Saudi Arabia held stakes of over 10% over the business.

  • "There is a genuine concern that this foreign influence could be exploited during political or diplomatic crises," Globes reports.
  • The deal in question, struck in February, would offer the Israeli government a golden share in ZIM, and promises to keep a presence in Israel while expanding the fleet there.
  • "We remain convinced that the concept is sound," Hapag-Lloyd wrote in a Monday statement.

The bottom line: A deal may still be struck, but investors aren't holding their breath. Shares of ZIM (NYSE: ZIM) sit at $28.67 apiece today — well below the $35 a share price Hapag-Lloyd has offered.
